subject: maths
pattern: Matrices usually carries 8-10 marks in the Karnataka 2nd PUC maths paper: 1-mark questions on order, symmetric and skew-symmetric, 2-3 mark questions on multiplication, transpose, symmetric/skew-symmetric decomposition and equations in A, and a 5-mark question on finding the inverse by elementary row operations (3x3) or proving the sum-of-symmetric-and-skew-symmetric theorem. Examiners expect each row operation to be written beside the matrix and the answer to be verified.

questions.q: Define a symmetric matrix and a skew-symmetric matrix.
questions.answer: A square matrix $A=[a_{ij}]$ is symmetric if $A'=A$, i.e. $a_{ij}=a_{ji}$ for all $i,j$. It is skew-symmetric if $A'=-A$, i.e. $a_{ij}=-a_{ji}$ for all $i,j$; in that case all diagonal elements are zero.

questions.q: If a matrix has 8 elements, what are the possible orders it can have?
questions.answer: The possible orders are all ordered pairs of factors of 8: $1\times8,\ 8\times1,\ 2\times4,\ 4\times2$. So there are four possible orders.

questions.q: If $A$ is a matrix of order $2\times3$ and $B$ is of order $3\times2$, write the orders of $AB$ and $BA$.
questions.answer: $AB$ has order $2\times2$ and $BA$ has order $3\times3$ (the number of columns of the first equals the number of rows of the second).

questions.q: Construct a $2\times2$ matrix $A=[a_{ij}]$ whose elements are given by $a_{ij}=\dfrac{(i+j)^2}{2}$.

questions.answer: $AB=\begin{bmatrix}1+4&0+2\\3+8&0+4\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}5&2\\11&4\end{bmatrix}$. $BA=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\2+3&4+4\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\5&8\end{bmatrix}$. Since $AB\neq BA$, matrix multiplication is not commutative.

questions.q: Show that $AA'$ is a symmetric matrix for any matrix $A$.
questions.answer: Let $P=AA'$. Then $P'=(AA')'=(A')'A'$ by the reversal law $(AB)'=B'A'$. Since $(A')'=A$, $P'=AA'=P$. Hence $AA'$ is symmetric.
By equality of matrices, $x+y=6$ and $xy=8$. So $x$ and $y$ are roots of $t^2-6t+8=0$, i.e. $(t-2)(t-4)=0$. Hence $(x,y)=(2,4)$ or $(4,2)$.

questions.q: Express $A=\begin{bmatrix}3&5\\1&-1\end{bmatrix}$ as the sum of a symmetric and a skew-symmetric matrix.

questions.answer: $AB=\begin{bmatrix}-1&2&1\\4&-8&-4\\-3&6&3\end{bmatrix}$, so $(AB)'=\begin{bmatrix}-1&4&-3\\2&-8&6\\1&-4&3\end{bmatrix}$. $B'=\begin{bmatrix}-1\\2\\1\end{bmatrix}$, $A'=\begin{bmatrix}1&-4&3\end{bmatrix}$, so $B'A'=\begin{bmatrix}-1&4&-3\\2&-8&6\\1&-4&3\end{bmatrix}$. Both are equal, hence $(AB)'=B'A'$.

$A^2=\begin{bmatrix}9-8&-6+4\\12-8&-8+4\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1&-2\\4&-4\end{bmatrix}$. $kA-2I=\begin{bmatrix}3k-2&-2k\\4k&-2k-2\end{bmatrix}$. Equating: $3k-2=1$ gives $k=1$; also $-2k=-2$, $4k=4$, $-2k-2=-4$ all hold. Hence $k=1$.

Using elementary row operations, find the inverse of $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&-2\\-1&3&0\\0&-2&1\end{bmatrix}$.
Prove that every square matrix can be expressed uniquely as the sum of a symmetric and a skew-symmetric matrix.
questions.answer: Let $A$ be a square matrix. Write $A=\tfrac12(A+A')+\tfrac12(A-A')=P+Q$. $P'=\tfrac12(A'+A)=P$, so $P$ is symmetric. $Q'=\tfrac12(A'-A)=-Q$, so $Q$ is skew-symmetric. Uniqueness: suppose $A=R+S$ with $R$ symmetric and $S$ skew-symmetric. Then $A'=R'+S'=R-S$. Adding, $A+A'=2R$ so $R=P$; subtracting, $A-A'=2S$ so $S=Q$. Hence the representation is unique.
